inline.s: Master Hanshan, a great manifestation of spiritual power. His merit in spreading the Dharma was deep, yet the jealous slandered him.
He was banished to guard Guangzhou, thereby warding off calamity. Fortunately there was a great official who looked on him with special regard.
He spread the Dharma at Caoxi, renewing the severed life of wisdom. Speaking the Dharma in accord with occasion, great abuses dissolved.
Protecting the country and comforting the people, his merit rose to the rank of an honored counselor. After his passing, his body remained, unrotted and unchanged.
Guangdong and Jiangxi contended, and he was carried back to the banks of Caoxi. The Sixth and Seventh Ancestors are proclaimed in the proverbs of the time.
He added luster to the sun of Buddha, serving as a moat and rampart for the Dharma. His writings are vast and broad, bright as sun and moon.
(In the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Inscription on the Six-Verse Handscroll of Master Hanshan)
The Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan says:

'Every year the pilgrims of Caoxi, in the second and eighth months, people from the whole province enter the mountain to pay homage; and after offering incense to the Sixth Ancestor, they say they will offer incense to the Seventh Ancestor — hence the title 'the Seventh Ancestor of Caoxi.'

blocks.text: 25. Returning by the Power of His Vow

inline.s: 'Hanshan's former vow was not yet fulfilled, so again he manifested birth as Jieliu
. He denounced those who cultivate the blessings of the human and heavenly realms, saying they are truly the peers of the icchantika and candala
(they are precisely the class of the icchantika and candala)

. The mind of Buddha and of my own self is originally no different; Buddha is already accomplished while I have not yet cultivated. If one would have mind and Buddha both without difference, one should seek it through recollecting and reciting the Buddha.'
(From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · the Tenth Patriarch of the Qing, Master Xingce of Puren Monastery, Yushan)

[Icchantika] The brief form of e-icchantika, meaning one who does not believe in cause and effect, commits the five heinous offences and the ten evil acts, cuts off all roots of good, and falls into the avici hell. [Candala (
)] The brief form of candala; here it denotes evil people.
[Those who cultivate the blessings of the human and heavenly realms]

In the later Essay on Urging the Arousal of True Faith, Master Xingce taught: without real faith, although one recites the Buddha's name and observes a pure diet, releases lives and cultivates merit, still one is only a good person of this world, who at the end of life is reborn in a good place and there enjoys bliss. While enjoying that bliss he then creates evil karma; and having created evil karma, he must fall into evil paths. Seen with right eyes, compared with the classes of the icchantika and candala, he is only a single step short.

After Master Wengong passed away, Master Xingce at Baoen Monastery met a fellow practitioner, Master Ying of Xi'an Hermitage, who urged him to cultivate the pure karma. Later he met Master Qiaoshi of Qiantang, who guided him to read the doctrine of the Tiantai school. He then entered a pure chamber together with Qiaoshi and practiced the Lotus samadhi. The wisdom of his past lives thereupon became suddenly clear, and he completely awakened to the essence of the Tiantai teaching.
In the second year of Kangxi

, he built a thatched hut on a small islet in the Western Creek of Fahua Mountain in Hangzhou, and there devoted himself solely to the Pure Land practice, and so named the place where he dwelt 'Fu-Lian Hermitage'
. In the ninth year of Kangxi
, he dwelt at Puren Monastery on Yushan, and advocated establishing a Pure Land Lotus Society, and those who followed gathered from all sides.

If one does not single-mindedly recollect that Buddha and seek rebirth in his land, one will surely drift along with karma and undergo immeasurable suffering. What is called

[Buddha in principle, Buddha in name] These are the first two of the six stages of Buddhahood. [Six stages of Buddhahood] The six stages that mark the course of a common being's practice up to Buddhahood:

, the Buddha in principle (the noumenal Buddha): all sentient beings, though they revolve in the six destinies and abide daily amid the dust of afflictions, turning their back on the awakened essence, yet the merit of Buddhahood is still fully present, so it is called 'the Buddha in principle.' Second, the Buddha in name: whether from a good teacher or from the scriptures, one hears that the very mind inherently possesses the unborn, undying Buddhahood, and through the name comprehends it, suddenly awakening, so it is called 'the Buddha in name.' Third, the Buddha in contemplation and practice: not only does one understand the name, but further one contemplates and practices according to the teaching; the mind's contemplation is clear, and the principle and wisdom correspond, so it is called 'the Buddha in contemplation and practice.'
(Here 'principle' is the object of contemplation, and 'wisdom' is the wisdom that contemplates; for 'correspond' means

fitting — that is, the realm and the wisdom are in accord, and words and deeds are consistent.) Fourth, the Buddha in near-resemblance: the practitioner at this stage, in contemplation, contemplates more and more clearly, and in stillness becomes more and more still; though not truly awakened and realized, yet he is near the principle, as though truly realized, so it is called 'the Buddha in near-resemblance.' Fifth, the Buddha in partial realization: this is after the ten stages of faith, when one breaks a portion of ignorance and realizes a portion of the three virtues, entering the first abiding stage and realizing the Dharma-body; from here one becomes a Dharma-body great being, and from the first abiding stage on, breaking ignorance and realizing the three virtues stage by stage up to equal enlightenment, passing through forty-one stages and breaking forty-one portions, so it is called 'the Buddha in partial realization.' Sixth, the Buddha in ultimate realization: from equal enlightenment one breaks the final portion of ignorance, and then delusion is exhausted and the true is pure, completely realizing the Tathāgata nature inherent in this very body and entering the stage of wondrous enlightenment to become a Buddha, so it is called 'the Buddha in ultimate realization.' [Three virtues] First, the virtue of the Dharma-body; second, the virtue of prajna; third, the virtue of liberation.

In these seven days of holding the name and reciting the Buddha, what is prized is a single-minded, unconfused state, unbroken and unmingled, not the swiftness and multitude of the recitation. One should be neither too slow nor too urgent, holding the name closely and closely, so that the Buddha-name in the heart is clear, distinctly perceived. Whether dressing or eating, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the one great name flows on continuously and unbroken, like the breath itself, neither scattered nor drowsy. Reciting the name with such single-minded diligence may be called the one who is able to practice the reliance-on-matter with single-minded vigor.

[What is called the one who is able to practice the reliance-on-matter with single-minded vigor] There is the Buddha-recitation of the matter and of the principle. The matter-recitation is to recite Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the principle-recitation is to probe one's own nature or to contemplate truly the reality of all dharmas. The matter-path is earnest toward rebirth; the principle-path aims at seeing the nature. The one-mind of matter and the one-mind of principle are also called the undivided mind of matter and the undivided mind of principle. Master Ouyi says:
'The one-mind of matter is distinctly clear, neither drowsy nor scattered; the one-mind of principle is the silent accord with the unborn and the clear penetration of one's own nature.'

(From the Collected Writings of the Master of Lingfeng, Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber) [Contemplating truly the reality of all dharmas] This is the Buddha-recitation of reality. [Four kinds of Buddha-recitation] First, holding the name: calling the Buddha-name. Second, contemplating an image: contemplating the Buddha's statue or picture. Third, contemplating the visualization: contemplate according to the Contemplation Sutra of Amitāyus. Fourth, Buddha-recitation of reality: contemplate truly the reality of all dharmas, which reality is precisely the Buddha's Dharma-body, and use the Dharma of 'ultimately empty, nothing existing' to recite the Buddha. (Concerning the reality of all dharmas, see

If one is a genuine seeker of the Way, one can directly probe that all dharmas are one and the same, and that there is no difference among them. That is to say, sentient beings and the buddhas are non-dual, oneself and others are non-dual, the retributions of the environment and of the body are non-dual, the pure and the defiled are non-dual, pleasure and suffering are non-dual, delight and aversion are non-dual, taking and rejecting are non-dual, enlightenment and affliction are non-dual, and birth-and-death and nirvana are non-dual. All of these two-fold dharmas are in reality of one and the same mark, equally pure.
[Probing that all dharmas are one and the same, with no difference among them] This is probing the reality of all dharmas, and is the Buddha-recitation of reality. The Buddha-Store Sutra says:
'What is called the reality of all dharmas? That is, all dharmas are, in the ultimate, empty, existing as nothing. With this Dharma of 'ultimately empty, nothing existing' one recites the Buddha.'

'To see nothing existing is called reciting the Buddha.' 'In such a Dharma, even a small thought cannot be obtained; this is called reciting the Buddha. Shariputra, this Dharma of reciting the Buddha cuts off the path of speech, goes beyond all thoughts, and cannot be thought of; this is called reciting the Buddha.'

) [The two retributions] The retribution of the environment and the retribution of the body. The lands, houses, implements, and so on of the world, as that on which the body relies, are called the 'retribution of the environment'; the body of a sentient being, made up of the five skandhas in temporary combination, as the recompense of past karma, is called the 'retribution of the body.'
One need not forcibly arrange anything to do; one simply probes truly by oneself:
All dharmas are thus, with no second mark.

When the probing reaches its utmost, it suddenly accords with one's own fundamental mind, and one realizes the undivided mind of principle. Then one knows that dressing and eating are always samadhi; laughing and scolding are none other than Buddha-work; and the one-mind and the scattered mind are in the end but idle talk. Throughout the two six-hour periods, if one perceives
that not a hair's breadth of a different mark is obtainable, then though one be mindful with utmost sincerity

call the name, it is the same as open scolding and reviling; and though one be diligent in cultivation, it is likewise an ascetic practice in a dream. Only when one is thus enlightened is he a genuine seeker of the Way, one who holds the name with single-minded vigor.

[All dharmas are thus] All dharmas are one and the same, with no difference. [Thus] The meaning of 'one and the same.' In Buddhism, the true, unchanging nature of all dharmas can hardly be described in words, so the word 'thus' is borrowed to represent it. The nature is the reality; the reality is the 'thus.' Because the true face of all dharmas is entirely the same, it is called 'thus.' [Fundamental mind] The original state of the mind. (For details see
The former kind of undivided mind

seems easy but is hard. As long as one is able to attain the undivided mind of matter, one will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. He who also attains the undivided mind of principle is reborn in the highest grade of the highest rebirth.

However, these two kinds of undivided mind are both things that ordinary people can do; anyone who has a mind can cultivate and learn them. The monks and laypeople together in this hall must not regard the undivided mind of principle as unattainably high, and so be content to dwell in a lowly state. Each should diligently spur on body and mind: nearer, within these seven days; farther, throughout a whole life, always holding this faith, always cultivating this practice. Even if one cannot realize the realm of accord with one's own fundamental mind, still the cause of rebirth is very superior, and the grade of transformation within the lotus bud will surely not be in the middle or lower.
If, after these seven days, one turns a deaf ear to the above instruction, and the familiar place
after all never becomes unfamiliar, and the unfamiliar place

remains hard to make familiar, and the ignorance and karmic habits entangle and interweave, vainly expecting to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss through the merit of this single vigorous seven-day retreat — while in these seven days one has not even

the state of the undivided mind of matter — this is precisely the 'few roots of goodness, blessings, and conditions.' How can rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss be hoped for? So that Shakyamuni Buddha's

in the Amitabha Sutra is instead suspected to be deceptive. Whose fault is this after all? Pure practitioners of the Buddha-retreat, may you each examine this and, being admonished by this instruction, take care to spur yourselves.

[The familiar after all never becomes unfamiliar, the unfamiliar remaining hard to make familiar] In practice, one must 'turn the unfamiliar to the familiar, and the familiar to the unfamiliar.' For a reciter of the Buddha, the unfamiliar recitation turns familiar, and the familiar attachment turns unfamiliar. [The golden-worded sincere utterance] The Buddha taught in the Amitabha Sutra:

'If there are good men or good women who, having heard of Amitābha Buddha, hold his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, with a single-minded, undistracted mind — then at the end of that person's life, Amitābha Buddha together with the holy assembly appears before him. When that person dies, his mind is not inverted, and he is instantly reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.'

Master Miaofeng's Dharma name was Fudeng, and his lay surname was Xu; he was a descendant of Xu Juju, a famous man of the Spring and Autumn period. In the nineteenth year of Jiajing of the Ming dynasty (C.E.

) he was born in a poor family in Pingyang Prefecture of Shanxi (present-day Linfen, Shanxi). At seven he met a year of famine and both his parents died of illness and hunger. At that time the family was so poor that even a thin coffin could not be bought; with the help of neighbors and relatives, two torn mats were used to wrap the bodies and the parents were buried carelessly.

After this Miaofeng became an orphan with no one to raise him, and every day he herded sheep for the villagers, barely keeping himself alive. In this way he grew to twelve, and really could not go on; he heard there was a Buddhist monastery nearby where one could shave the head and become a monk, cultivating and observing a pure diet. This too was a way out for a poor boy, and so he ran off and left the home life.

In the middle of the Ming dynasty, Buddhism was in decline, and many monasteries had in fact nothing of precepts and practice to speak of; monastics too were ranked in grades, the rich like landlords and merchants, the poor like hired laborers and tenant farmers, and oppression, exploitation, and discrimination were common. Unfortunately Miaofeng entered just such a pit of fire: poor, ugly, young, and weak, he was bullied everywhere. Not to speak of receiving precepts and studying the Dharma and practicing, even coarse food and tattered clothes could not be assured. Miaofeng muddled along painfully for five years and, seeing himself at seventeen, with nothing accomplished and growing more and more difficult, he simply ran away, taking a broken gourd as a beggar's bowl and wandering the rivers and lakes.

Wandering from Pingyang to Puzhou (present-day Yongji city), he stopped running about. By day he begged in Puzhou city, and by night slept in the Wenchang Pavilion. The old monk Langgong of Wenchang Pavilion was a true practitioner with a mind of compassion, and treated Miaofeng well, often looking after him. Gradually, Miaofeng's fate took a turn for the better.

blocks.text: The Favor of the Prince of Shanyin

inline.s: In Puzhou city there dwelt a prince of the imperial clan of the Ming, the Prince of Shanyin, whose surname was Zhu and name Junshan. His ancestor was the thirteenth son of the founding emperor Taizu, Zhu Gui, the Prince of Dai, enfeoffed at Datong; after several generations the clan multiplied, and since life in Datong was difficult a few branches moved to southern Shanxi. The Prince of Shanyin, Zhu Junshan, was such a collateral minor prince, an ordinary noble. The history records of him: 'In the twentieth year of Wanli (

), when the Western Xia was unruly, the Prince of Shanyin, Junshan, submitted eight chapters of poems, which carried the intent of remonstrance. Since the Dai lineage dwelt at the frontier and its branches had passed through calamity again and again, his words were all deeply concerned and far-sighted, beyond even what the court officials of the middle kingdom could reach.' We can see that he was an enlightened noble with a sense of concern, and had literary talent and believed in Buddhism. Because of his favorable regard, the life of Master Miaofeng was changed.

One day the Prince of Shanyin saw Miaofeng in the Wenchang Pavilion, and saw that this young man, though he was extremely ugly and every feature apparent, had a focused spirit and solid bones — a makable talent — so he hinted to Master Langgong to look after Miaofeng. After a while a great earthquake struck southern Shanxi, and Puzhou was in ruins; Miaofeng too was crushed under a collapsed house, and Langgong dug him out, finding that his skin and flesh were unharmed. As the saying goes: 'He who survives a great disaster is destined for future fortune.' The Prince of Shanyin therefore regarded Miaofeng even more favorably, judging that he would surely become a great vessel, and so deliberately nurtured him.

The Prince of Shanyin said to Miaofeng: 'You have escaped a great disaster; why not earnestly reflect on the great matter of birth and death and begin your practice early?' Miaofeng was now twenty-one, and hearing this wished to travel far to seek learning. The Prince of Shanyin thought Miaofeng's foundation in Buddhism too thin, and that he could not learn much by going out, so he had him go to the Qiyan Monastery on Zhongtiao Mountain nearby to practice in 'seclusion.' Qiyan Monastery had been the place where the eminent monk Tanyan of the Northern Dynasties first rose to prominence, and by then it had fallen into ruin; the Prince of Shanyin helped Miaofeng repair a few rooms to dwell in.

So-called 'seclusion' means to shut the door and not come out, concentrating energy on practice, while the needs of life are cared for by a 'guardian.' Miaofeng asked a nearby Dharma master about the practice method of the 'Realm of Dharmas' contemplation, and began the long 'seclusion.' This method requires one to practice always standing, not allowed to sit or sleep for several years, and is extremely hard. Miaofeng persisted for three years, then suddenly had some awakening, and joyfully wrote four lines of verse on paper, entrusting someone to deliver them to the Prince of Shanyin for his verification. The Prince of Shanyin read them, wondered exceedingly, and judged that Miaofeng truly had spiritual faculties and far-seeing insight. But on reflection he thought that Miaofeng was still too young, and that if he were not subjected to checks and tempering, he might in time become an arrogant, vain, word-deceiving wild monk. The Prince had a flash of inspiration, made someone find an old shoe, cut off the smelly sole, put it in an envelope, and added a sheet of paper writing: 'This smelly shoe-sole, I seal and send to you; not for any other thing, but only to strike that mouth that makes verse!' and sent it back to Miaofeng. When Miaofeng saw it he immediately understood the Prince's deep intent, and before the Buddha earnestly bowed several times, and taking a thread, tied the smelly shoe-sole and hung it about his neck as a 'motto,' continuing his hard practice, and from then on never uttered rash opinions. After another three years the 'seclusion' came to an end, and he came out to pay respects to the Prince of Shanyin, carrying himself with the dignity of an eminent monk in his movements and speech.

The Prince of Shanyin continued to encourage Miaofeng: 'Though your practice now has some foundation, you have not yet heard true Dharma, and if you are not careful you may in time fall into wrong views. Now there is an eminent monk in Jieshan preaching the Shurangama Sutra; I will provide a bit of travel money, and you should go listen.' Miaofeng was twenty-seven that year, went to Jieshan to hear the sutra, and received the full precepts, gaining greatly. After returning to Puzhou, the Prince of Shanyin again said: 'You may now be counted a qualified monk, but beyond the mountain there are mountains and beyond the sky there is a sky; if your steps never leave the monastery gate, you are still like a frog at the bottom of a well with no knowledge. There are many eminent Dharma masters of the South; go and travel and visit them, and broaden your horizons. When you return, tell me all about it in detail — consider it a hard journey taken on my behalf.'

The Prince of Shanyin personally prepared the implements and travel money for Miaofeng's wandering pilgrimage, and took off the woolen clothes and stockings he himself wore, and over them sewed a layer of humble torn cloth, and gave them to Miaofeng to keep warm on the road.
Miaofeng then traveled alone, wandering among the clouds and waters, visiting the eminent masters of the South to seek their instruction, and made a pilgrimage to Putuo Mountain of the South Sea.

The wandering pilgrimage of a monastic is very hard work. When one chanced upon a temple one would lodge and take a pure meal; when not, one ate and slept in the open. Miaofeng came down from Putuo Mountain, crossed the sea back to Ningbo, and unfortunately contracted the epidemic rife there, lying ill in an inn. Alone, with no one to look after him. At night he wanted a sip of water, but though he called for a long time the inn servant did not answer. Half dead with thirst, he remembered there was a little water in the washbasin, and forcing his sick body, he scooped a few mouthfuls with his hand. The bathwater entered his mouth, and it tasted utterly sweet. In the morning he rose, and looking in the light, saw the basin actually held filthy, stinking water; at once sickened and disgusted, he vomited for a long time.

But in the life of a monastic all things require awakening to Buddhist principle. When Miaofeng had finished vomiting, he suddenly thought: last night when he was terribly thirsty the water was sweet, but in the morning, when the light was plain, the water turned out to be dirty — it seems 'purity and defilement come from the mind'! He understood this principle at once, immediately no longer felt the nausea and vomiting, his heart was relieved, and his illness soon healed, though he was left covered in yellow swellings and itching sores.

Next he wandered to Nanjing and lodged temporarily at Tianjie Monastery. The monks of the monastery, seeing that he was ugly and dirty, assigned him a duty of cleaning the latrines, what in the monastery (that is, the temple) is called the 'clean-head.' Through this connection he made the acquaintance of Master Hanshan Deqing, later called one of the four great masters of the late Ming.

The meeting of the two was very interesting. Hanshan was younger than Miaofeng, but he came from Baoen Monastery, a great monastery of the nation, and was a disciple of a distinguished house, an emerging talent. Moreover his talent overflowed and his bearing was elegant, so his fame was already on high at the time. Master Wuji lectured on the Lotus Sutra at Tianjie Monastery, and Hanshan served as a co-lecturer, comparable to a 'teaching assistant' — a post that drew much attention. Yet Hanshan was not content with preaching the sutra; in secret he often sought out extraordinary people, wishing to probe the 'one final stroke upward.' Every morning when he went to the latrine, he found that this latrine of Tianjie Monastery was very clean, yet he never saw anyone sweeping it, and thinking it strange, he pondered that there must be a person of worth. So he deliberately spied for several days, and found that the 'clean-head' who cleaned the latrine was a sick practitioner with yellow swellings, who every night lit a lamp and worked, and by the early hours when the monks rose to use the latrine, his work was already done. So Hanshan concluded that this sick practitioner with yellow swellings was a person of worth, and resolved to befriend him.

After a few days the latrine suddenly was not clean. Hanshan asked about it, and learned that the 'clean-head' had fallen ill, so he went to see him, and by this he became acquainted with Master Miaofeng. The conversation when the two met was also quite interesting. Miaofeng said: 'The sickness of the body I can still bear; it is the sickness of craving that is hard to cure.' Hanshan asked him why; Miaofeng said: 'When I see others eating steamed buns, my heart cannot put it down.' Hanshan knew Miaofeng had gone hungry too long — an outside sick monk, not valued in the monastery, hungry and no one looking after him — so he found some pastries and gave them to Miaofeng, who ate them very happily, and by this the two established a sincere friendship.
